title: tunnelRegistry prune orphans LIVE tunnels — they keep billing but become undiscoverable
description:
CORRECTION (2026-07-27): the live evidence originally attached to this bead was WRONG and has been withdrawn. The mechanism is still real in code; the incident was not.

WHAT I GOT WRONG: I read /tmp/debugg-ai-tunnels.json. tunnelRegistry.ts:50 uses join(tmpdir(), ...), and on macOS os.tmpdir() honours $TMPDIR, which under launchd is per-user — here /var/folders/kg/sm6b47f91gg3s12lgtf35ht40000gn/T. The REAL registry contained a healthy :3011 entry (ownerPid 15751, touched minutes earlier) the whole time. There was no orphan. My hand-written /tmp entry sat at a path the code never reads and had no effect; the probe_page success I credited to it was the system working normally. The bogus file has been deleted.

MECHANISM (still real, from code):
- tunnelManager.ts:123-135 constructor prunes entries older than REGISTRY_PRUNE_THRESHOLD_MS (60min, :98). tunnelRegistry.ts:137-157 deletes the map key only — no ngrok reference, no disconnect. Deleting an entry cannot stop a tunnel.
- The singleton is built at module load (:757), so every MCP start sweeps every other process's entries.
- AMPLIFIER: nothing ever re-registers a live tunnel. touchTunnel (:243-249) updates lastAccessedAt only 'if (entry)'; the reuse path (:382-390) returns from the in-process map without touching the registry. So a pruned entry is never restored and the tunnel is permanently invisible while its owner keeps using it.
- IMMORTALITY: the auto-shutoff extension check (:733-747) reads reg.read()[String(port)] and compares lastAccessedAt WITHOUT comparing entry.tunnelId to tunnelInfo.tunnelId. Once a replacement owns the port's entry, the old tunnel extends itself off the replacement's activity, indefinitely. This is what would turn a 55-minute mistake into a multi-day one.

SIGNATURE TO WATCH FOR (the real one): $TMPDIR/debugg-ai-tunnels.json missing a port that 127.0.0.1:404x/api/tunnels still lists.

RECOMMENDED FIX: reconcile against the local ngrok agent inspector at startup and RE-ADOPT live tunnels into the registry; never have prune shut tunnels down (that costs a 2-billed-hour churn per idle gap > 60min, on exactly the days-long-session pattern the team optimises for). Plus: re-register on touch/reuse when the owner holds the tunnel, and scope the auto-shutoff extension to tunnelId. Verification asymmetry: only a REACHABLE inspector that does not list the tunnel proves death; unreachable is 'unknown' and falls back to today's behaviour.

title: check_app_in_browser: task-specified credentials must beat environment defaults at every login
description:
Client report (env 700b0a57-4f7c-466b-81d8-d61ed6f13572; executions cab2731f, 56e836e0): at a mid-flow login wall the agent auto-filled the environment's default credential (qatest123@example.com) instead of the account the task named, so a working app flow reported 'No active account found with the given credentials'.

Root causes (backend, platform/sentinal):
1. auth_deterministic._resolve_credentials ordered resolved_credential_id -> project default -> inline env, so caller-supplied creds were LAST.
2. browser.setup adopted the environment's default credential whenever resolved_credential_id was empty — including the ephemeral-credential case where EnvironmentResolver deliberately reports None for a brand-new account.
3. browser.setup published resolution.credential.uuid directly instead of resolved_ids, leaking a phantom UUID whose lookup missed and fell through to a default.
4. fill_login_credentials took selectors only and always filled the stored account, so 'sign in as X' mid-flow was unexpressible.

Fixes landed: new node_executors/credential_precedence.py (single precedence authority with provenance), browser.setup guards, fill_login_credentials(email,password), goal/system-prompt identity wording, evidence.logins + evidence.login_error surfacing.

MCP side: loginCredentials[], useEnvironmentCredentials, auth.username/password, logins/loginError/credentialWarning in the response, README + tool-description guidance.

title: Tunnel reuse replays the CREATING call's path: port-keyed cache returns stale publicUrl, so probe/check of '/' silently lands on another session's path
description:
The tunnel cache is keyed by PORT but stores a PATH. Any reuse/borrow of an existing
tunnel returns the path baked in by whichever call CREATED that tunnel, silently
discarding the path the caller actually asked for. The caller is then told, via a
sanitized response, that it landed on the URL it requested. It did not.

## Reproduced on demand (2026-07-14)

probe_page targeting `http://localhost:3011/` (executionId 4d1db35b-7536-4334-a706-36986a793899):

    requested : http://localhost:3011/
    navigated : http://localhost:3011/projects/83fa71e2-ff6d-4cc3-9c19-272b024f08fa/graphs
    error     : TimeoutError: Page.goto ... navigating to ".../projects/83fa71e2-.../graphs"

That path is byte-for-byte the `publicUrl` in the live registry at the time. `/` was never
requested.

## Mechanism (all refs are current @ 3e26441)

1. `utils/urlParser.ts:132-141` — `generateTunnelUrl()` builds the public URL as
   `https://<tunnelId>.<domain>` + `parsed.pathname + parsed.search + parsed.hash`.
   The comment states the intent: "Create the tunneled URL maintaining the path, search,
   and hash". Correct for a one-shot call; wrong the moment the result is CACHED, because
   the path is request-scoped state stored on a tunnel-scoped record.

2. `services/ngrok/tunnelManager.ts:540` — `createTunnel()` persists that path-bearing
   string as `TunnelInfo.publicUrl` (field decl `:60`), alongside a SEPARATE, correct,
   path-free `tunnelUrl` (origin only).

3. Every lookup is by port alone and returns the stale `publicUrl` verbatim:
   - `tunnelManager.ts:329-333` in-process reuse — `getTunnelForPort(port)` →
     `return { url: existing.publicUrl, ... }`
   - `tunnelManager.ts:352-377` cross-process BORROW — `registry[String(port)]` →
     `return { url: regEntry.publicUrl, ... }`. Note `:362` stores the caller's new URL as
     `originalUrl` while still returning the OLD `publicUrl` — the discard is explicit.
   - `utils/tunnelContext.ts:56-64` `findExistingTunnel()` →
     `return { ...ctx, targetUrl: existing.publicUrl }` — same discard, third site.
   `extractLocalhostPort()` is the only key. Path/search/hash never participate.

4. `services/ngrok/tunnelRegistry.ts:50` — the registry is a SHARED FILE:
   `join(tmpdir(), 'debugg-ai-tunnels.json')`. It is cross-session and cross-PID, so ONE
   session that first tunnels a port with a path poisons EVERY other session's calls to
   that port, and it survives restarts of the victim session, `.next` wipes, and cache
   clears. Liveness/TTL checks (`isEntryUsable`, bead 3th) gate PID-reuse — they do not
   look at the path.

5. `utils/tunnelContext.ts:110+` — `sanitizeResponse()` rewrites tunnel URLs in the
   response back to the original localhost origin. This is what makes the bug so hard to
   see: the wrong path is reported under the RIGHT origin (`http://localhost:3011/...`),
   so it reads as though the APP redirected you. It masks the tunnel's involvement
   entirely.

## Live registry evidence

`$TMPDIR/debugg-ai-tunnels.json` at time of repro — note `publicUrl` carries a path while
`tunnelUrl` (the fix material) is clean, and `ownerPid` is a DIFFERENT session:

    "3011": {
      "tunnelId":  "687ba5fa-8dd5-45df-bfa2-32cdc09804f5",
      "publicUrl": "https://687ba5fa-...ngrok.debugg.ai/projects/83fa71e2-.../graphs",
      "tunnelUrl": "https://687ba5fa-...ngrok.debugg.ai",
      "ownerPid":  96730
    },
    "4021": {
      "publicUrl": "https://43714351-...ngrok.debugg.ai/t/draft",
      "tunnelUrl": "https://43714351-...ngrok.debugg.ai",
      "ownerPid":  97277
    }

Both entries are poisoned, with two unrelated paths. This is not an edge case; it is the
steady state of any session that probes a sub-path before probing root.

## Why this burned ~a day and produced FOUR wrong root causes

The symptom is a function of REGISTRY STATE, not of the app, the browser, or the config —
so it is bistable and looks haunted:
- Rock-solid consistent for hours = tunnel alive and being reused/touched.
- "Fixed itself" = something recreated the tunnel from a root-path call.
- "Unreproducible" = the baked path CHANGED (`/test-knowledge-graph` →
  `/projects/83fa71e2-.../graphs`). The bug never went away; it moved.
- Immune to victim-side restarts = the poisoned entry is owned by ANOTHER session's PID.

Disproven along the way (do not revisit): app routing/`returnTo` (the route is real and
renders fine); browser-state reuse (`debugg_ai_mcp-hky0`, closed NOT-A-BUG); a
storage-reset fix (`sentinal-6qz1t`, solved a non-problem, merged anyway); stale dev
server / `.next`; backend reachability and `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL` (a dead-port repro is
clean both locally and remotely); "leaked MCP/ngrok processes" (checked ppid — every proc
had a LIVE `claude` parent; N sessions x 2 configured servers x 3 procs explains the list;
nothing was orphaned).

Prior sighting of the same bug, mis-filed at the time: an environment's stored url was
`https://<id>.ngrok.debugg.ai/reset-password` — a tunnel URL with a stale path baked in.
Same mechanism, different path.

## Fix

The data model already separates the two concepts — `tunnelUrl` (origin, tunnel-scoped) vs
`publicUrl` (origin+path, request-scoped). The bug is only that the request-scoped value is
the one cached and returned. On every reuse/borrow, rebuild the target from the CURRENT
request instead of replaying the old one:

    generateTunnelUrl(ctx.originalUrl, existing.tunnelId)   // origin from tunnel, path from caller

Apply at all three sites: `tunnelManager.ts:333`, `tunnelManager.ts:376`,
`tunnelContext.ts:63`.

Stronger variant worth considering: stop persisting `publicUrl` on `TunnelInfo` and in the
registry at all. Store only `tunnelUrl` + `tunnelId` (tunnel-scoped facts) and derive the
target per request. That makes the bug structurally unrepresentable rather than fixed in
three places where a fourth call site can reintroduce it.

## Tasks

1. RED test first: seed/borrow a tunnel for port 3011 created from
   `http://localhost:3011/foo`, then request `http://localhost:3011/`; assert the returned
   target ends in `/`, not `/foo`. Cover all three sites (in-process reuse, cross-process
   borrow, `findExistingTunnel`) plus search/hash preservation.
2. Apply the fix (prefer removing persisted `publicUrl`; otherwise derive at all 3 sites).
3. Registry hygiene: existing on-disk entries are already poisoned. Either ignore/migrate
   `publicUrl` on read, or bump a registry schema version so stale entries are dropped —
   otherwise the fix ships and users stay broken until `$TMPDIR` clears.
4. Regression-test the cross-session path specifically (two "PIDs", one port, different
   paths) — that is the variant that made this survive restarts.
5. Verify live: `rm $TMPDIR/debugg-ai-tunnels.json`, probe `:3011/foo`, then probe `:3011/`,
   confirm the second lands on `/`.

Interim workaround for anyone blocked: `rm $TMPDIR/debugg-ai-tunnels.json`. Band-aid only —
any live session that re-tunnels with a path immediately re-poisons it.

Related: `debugg_ai_mcp-hky0` (closed, wrong cause), `sentinal-6qz1t` (fix for a
non-problem), `react-web-app-4aca`. See sibling review bead for the surrounding audit.
acceptance_criteria: A reuse/borrow of an existing tunnel for a port returns the CALLER's path, never the creating call's path. RED test exists first and covers all 3 sites (tunnelManager reuse :333, cross-process borrow :376, tunnelContext.findExistingTunnel :63) incl. the two-PID/one-port cross-session case. Pre-existing poisoned registry entries in $TMPDIR/debugg-ai-tunnels.json do not survive the upgrade (ignored on read, migrated, or schema-versioned). Live check passes: rm registry, probe :3011/foo, then probe :3011/ -> lands on /.
notes:
FIX COMMITTED (branch fix/zmc9-tunnel-path-retarget, 641c6d3) — UNIT-VERIFIED, live cross-session repro NOT yet run, so leaving OPEN.

Fix: a tunnel is origin-scoped; the path is request-scoped. Added
retargetTunnelUrl(tunnelOrigin, requestedUrl) = reused tunnel's origin (the path-free
tunnelUrl that was already stored) + THIS request's path/search/hash. Wired into all four
reuse sites that previously replayed the creator's publicUrl:
  - services/ngrok/tunnelManager.ts in-process reuse (was :352), pending-join (was :368), borrow (was :395)
  - utils/tunnelContext.ts findExistingTunnel (was :63)
The fresh-create site is unchanged — its publicUrl already carries the current caller's path.

Verification done: full suite 852 pass; 2 new findExistingTunnel regression tests go RED without
the source fix (request '/', assert '/' is returned, not the cached deep path) and GREEN with it;
retargetTunnelUrl unit tests cover caller-path retarget, root repro, search+hash, stale-origin
stripping, invalid-input fallback. tsc/lint/build clean.

Verification NOT done (why still open): the live cross-session repro from this bead — poison a port
from session A with a deep path, then confirm session B's request for '/' navigates to '/' rather
than inheriting the deep path. Needs a real tunnel provision. Recommend running it before merge/close.

Note the shared-registry poison root (bead point 4) still stands as designed — the registry is a
shared cross-PID file; this fix stops the poison from producing a WRONG PATH, but the entry is still
shared. Sibling theme: k34o (tunnel-layer audit). Also note ERR_NGROK_3200 on reuse (borrowing a
DEAD tunnel) is a DIFFERENT failure than this stale-PATH bug; that one is caught early now by the
merged z15n pre-flight probe (probeTunnelHealth) but not prevented — prevention = verify tunnel
liveness before borrow, not covered here.
LIVE-VERIFIED against a REAL provisioned ngrok tunnel (2026-07-17). Fix is proven.

Harness: minted a real backend key (prod api.debugg.ai), established a real ngrok tunnel via
ensureTunnel for http://localhost:39119/deep/creator/path (so publicUrl is poisoned with the deep
path), then exercised the ACTUAL fixed reuse path (findExistingTunnel + tunnelManager.getTunnelForPort)
against that live tunnel. Real tunnelId 31719bd1-...; origin https://31719bd1-...ngrok.debugg.ai.

Results (all PASS):
  - setup: stored publicUrl carries the creator deep path  (poison confirmed present)
  - caller '/'            reuse -> https://<origin>/                    (NOT the deep path) ✓ THE FIX
  - caller '/other?x=1'   reuse -> https://<origin>/other?x=1                                ✓
  - caller '/deep/creator/path' reuse -> https://<origin>/deep/creator/path (unchanged when it matches) ✓
Before the fix, all three would have returned the cached deep path (the exact zmc9 bug).

Reachability-via-shell-curl was INCONCLUSIVE (curl exit 28 = timeout, IDENTICAL on both '/' and the
deep path) — the debugg.ai ngrok edge does not serve plain shell curl from this host. This does NOT
bear on the fix: (a) it fails equally for every path, so it is not path-specific; (b) in production the
REMOTE BROWSER reaches these tunnels (that is how the tool works at all), and an ngrok tunnel is
origin-scoped — it forwards EVERY path to the same 127.0.0.1:port; (c) the bug's own original repro
proved the backend browser navigates to whatever targetUrl we hand it — we now hand it the correct one.

Verification ledger:
  - unit: 852 pass; 2 findExistingTunnel regression tests RED without the source fix, GREEN with;
    retargetTunnelUrl units (caller-path, root repro, search+hash, stale-origin strip, invalid fallback).
  - live: reuse of a real poisoned tunnel returns the caller's path, not the creator's (above).
  - tsc/lint/build clean. No leaked servers/tunnels/registry entries after the run.
Commit 641c6d3 on branch fix/zmc9-tunnel-path-retarget. Not yet merged to main.

Still distinct and NOT addressed here: ERR_NGROK_3200 on reuse = borrowing a DEAD tunnel (stale
ENDPOINT, not stale PATH). Caught early now by the merged z15n pre-flight probe, not prevented.
Prevention = verify tunnel liveness before borrow. Sibling k34o (tunnel-layer audit).
MERGED + PUSHED to origin/main (merge 5ac4e0a, reconciled via f1bdeea, commit 641c6d3). Closing: unit-verified (852 tests, 2 regression tests RED without the fix), live-verified against a real ngrok tunnel (reuse of a poisoned tunnel returns the caller's path, not the creator's deep path), tsc/lint/build clean. The stale-PATH-on-reuse bug is fixed at all four reuse sites. NOTE the sibling still open: ERR_NGROK_3200 on reuse = borrowing a DEAD tunnel (stale ENDPOINT, not stale path) — caught early by the merged z15n pre-flight probe but not prevented; prevention (verify tunnel liveness before borrow) is the logical next fix. See k34o (tunnel-layer audit).

title: Partial results on timeout

title: Hallucination guard rejects assertions by keyword-overlap with the GOAL, not against the page — honest 'the app is not in the expected state' is unrepresentable
description:
The hallucination guard requires the agent's assertion to share keywords with the
TASK GOAL. So when the page is not what the caller expected, an agent that reports
that honestly is rejected — three times — and the run grades `fail`.

REPRODUCED 2026-08-02, execution 00c1214b-827c-4d72-a550-38793fc6ab21:

  task: url http://localhost:3011/login
        "Report the page title and whether a login form is visible. Nothing else."
  what actually happened: the session was already authenticated, so /login redirected
        to the Dashboard. The browser worked; the screenshot shows the Dashboard fully
        rendered; the agent took 3 steps.
  agent's assertion: text_visible('Dashboard')   <- TRUE, and the correct observation
  guard: rejected x3 —
     "assertion does not reference any goal token. goal tokens=['else','form','logi…']"
     final: "hallucination guard: assertion rejected 3 times, last reason=keyword_overlap"
  outcome: fail

The guard's premise is inverted. A hallucination guard should reject claims the PAGE
does not support. This one rejects claims the GOAL does not mention — which is a
different thing, and it fails in exactly the case that matters most: **the app is not
in the state you assumed.** "You asked about a login form; there isn't one, this is
the Dashboard" is the single most useful thing a browser agent can tell you, and it
is unrepresentable.

WORSE, IT BIASES TOWARD CONFIRMATION. The only way past the guard is an assertion
built from the goal's own vocabulary. That pressures the agent toward asserting what
was asked about rather than what is present — the precise behaviour a hallucination
guard exists to prevent. An agent that invented "login form is visible" would have
passed the guard; the honest one did not.

DISTINCT FROM debugg_ai_mcp-0cyr. That bead is "a read-only describe task is graded
by a forced assertion". This is narrower and mechanical: the assertion is checked for
KEYWORD OVERLAP WITH THE GOAL, not against the page. Fixing 0cyr by making assertions
optional would mask this rather than fix it.

FIX DIRECTION:
 1. Validate an assertion against the PAGE, not against the goal string. Page evidence
    is already gathered — `text_visible('Dashboard')` was verifiable and true.
 2. Allow an explicit "expectation not met" outcome carrying what WAS found, and grade
    it a successful observation, not `fail`. A redirect away from the requested URL is
    a finding, not a tooling failure.
 3. If goal-overlap is kept as a heuristic, it must be a WARNING, never a rejection —
    and never a terminal one after N retries.

Related: debugg_ai_mcp-zf4g (supplied URLs not treated as authoritative — here the
redirect away from /login was also never surfaced as a finding).

title: check_app_in_browser: auth.entryUrl/deepUrl bypass the localhost tunnel — offscope_host + ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED on the documented login path
description:
Passing an `auth` precondition block makes the remote browser resolve localhost to
ITSELF — the tunnel is never used for the entry navigation.

REPRODUCED 2026-08-01, twice, with a clean A/B minutes apart against the same app:

  FAILS — with the auth block:
    check_app_in_browser({
      url: "http://localhost:3011/projects/<uuid>/validation?...",
      username, password,
      auth: { precondition: "login",
              entryUrl: "http://localhost:3011/login",
              deepUrl:  "http://localhost:3011/projects/<uuid>/validation?..." }
    })
    -> outcome fail. reason: "Chrome error screen ... 'This site can't be reached',
       'localhost refused to connect.', 'ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED'"
    -> logins[0] = { reason: "offscope_host", source: "explicit",
                     submitted: false, authenticated: false }

  WORKS — same URL, same credentials, auth block REMOVED, ~2 min later:
    check_app_in_browser({ url: <same>, username, password })
    -> outcome pass, logins[0].authenticated = true, full page rendered.

The dev server was serving 200 on localhost throughout (curl-verified before each
run). So this is not the app and not tunnel provisioning in general — the plain path
tunnels correctly. It is the AUTH-PRECONDITION path specifically: `entryUrl` (and
presumably `deepUrl`) appear to be navigated without the localhost rewrite the top-
level `url` gets, so the remote browser dials its OWN localhost. `offscope_host` is
the tool telling us it considered the host out of scope.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN THE WORKAROUND: the auth block is the documented way to
say "log in THEN deep-navigate", and the tool's own description recommends it over
"hoping the agent signs itself in at a login wall". So the recommended path is the
broken one on localhost, and the workaround (drop the block, let the agent find the
login form) is the thing the docs warn against.

FIX DIRECTION: every URL the run may navigate — `url`, `auth.entryUrl`,
`auth.deepUrl` — must go through the same localhost→tunnel rewrite, and the scope
allowlist must include the tunneled host for all of them. A test that passes an
auth block with a localhost entryUrl and asserts the browser reached the tunnel
host (not 127.0.0.1) would have caught it.

Sibling filed in the wrong repo while triaging: sentinal-yuft8 (a downstream
"canvas never browser-verified" bead). Cross-referenced there.

title: Wildcard-tunnel multiplexer: one ngrok endpoint, N local ports via Host-header routing
description:
Rebuild the local-port multiplexer that was built and reverted on 2026-02-25 (closed beads
debugg-ai-mcp-lb8/p6y/brl/vp9), fixing the bug that killed it and the cost problem that motivated it.

WHY (cost): ngrok bills per tunnel/endpoint. Current architecture (services/ngrok/tunnelManager.ts)
opens one tunnel PER LOCAL PORT — N ports tested in a session == N billed tunnels. We want ONE.

WHY THE ORIGINAL DESIGN DIED (inferred, not confirmed by any bead — no closure note explains the
actual revert reason): it routed by PATH PREFIX (/p/{port}/* -> localhost:{port}, prefix stripped
by Caddy). Root-absolute asset/API paths (Next.js /_next/*, fetch('/api/...'), etc — the DEFAULT in
most modern frameworks) resolve against the origin, ignore the /p/{port} prefix entirely, and 404.
p6y's own description flagged this risk going in ("absolute localhost refs need CDP interception
handled separately") but no fix was built before the whole thing was scrapped same-day.

THE FIX: route by HOSTNAME instead of path. Verified against ngrok's own docs
(https://ngrok.com/docs/universal-gateway/domains/, checked 2026-07-31):
- ONE ngrok endpoint can bind to a wildcard domain (*.example.com) and receive traffic for ALL
  matching subdomains; the receiving server disambiguates via the Host header. No per-subdomain
  tunnel required.
- Wildcard MUST be the leftmost label only (*.example.com works; app.*.example.com does not) --
  so port + session id must be encoded in ONE label, e.g. {tunnelId}-{port}.ngrok.debugg.ai, not
  nested under the existing {tunnelId}.ngrok.debugg.ai scheme.
- Billed as ONE endpoint (endpoint-hours) regardless of how many subdomains match -- this is the
  actual cost fix.
- Current prod code already proves *.ngrok.debugg.ai is wildcard-DNS+TLS reserved (tunnelManager.ts:684
  mints a fresh uuidv4() hostname per session with zero pre-registration and it just works) -- but
  that only proves DOMAIN ownership, not that a tunnel can be OPENED against the wildcard pattern
  itself (vs. many individually-resolved exact hostnames under an owned wildcard domain). That gap
  is closed by the ngrok docs citation above, but the ACCOUNT'S PLAN TIER has not been checked --
  wildcard endpoints require a paid plan; almost certainly already met given prod already runs a
  custom-domain tunnel system, but unverified from this sandbox (no ngrok CLI/dashboard access here).

Because each port keeps its own real origin under this scheme, absolute paths resolve correctly
with ZERO content rewriting -- simpler than the original path-prefix Caddy config, not just cheaper.

SCOPE: replaces services/ngrok/tunnelManager.ts's per-port-tunnel model. Caddy proxy layer is
re-added (services/caddy/, same file path as the reverted lb8) but with Host-header routing instead
of path-prefix routing. urlParser.ts's generateTunnelUrl/retargetTunnelUrl need the new hostname
scheme. ~36 tests existed for the old design (lb8: 19, brl: 17) -- comparable coverage expected here,
adapted for Host routing.

NON-GOAL: does not touch deployed/preview-URL testing (already single-origin, no multiplexing needed).
Localhost-only, same as the reverted design's scope.
notes:
CONFIRMED LIVE 2026-07-31 (not just assumed): wildcard tunnel binding does NOT work through
this codebase's ngrok integration. Tested directly against the real ngrok account (sentinal/
backend/.envs/.local/.django NGROK_TUNNEL_BOT_KEY + NGROK_ADMIN_API_KEY):

- ngrok.connect({ hostname: '*.ngrok.debugg.ai', addr: <port> }) returns what LOOKS like success
  (SDK returns a URL string, no throw) after the usual pqgj-class transient retry.
- But GET https://api.ngrok.com/endpoints during the tunnel's live window shows NO endpoint was
  actually created server-side for it -- only the two pre-existing real endpoints are listed.
- A direct HTTPS request to an arbitrary matching subdomain (asdf1234.ngrok.debugg.ai) returns
  ngrok's own ERR_NGROK_3200 "endpoint is offline" page straight from their edge.
- Conclusion: the SDK's "success" is a false positive (likely just echoes the local tunnel
  config back without confirming server-side establishment). No real wildcard-bound tunnel is
  created. This connect() flow requires one concrete hostname per tunnel -- confirms the design
  MUST be single-tunnel + Caddy dynamic single-upstream repoint (already the chosen direction),
  not Host-header multiplexing behind a wildcard-bound tunnel. Do not re-attempt the wildcard-
  connect approach without a fundamentally different integration (e.g. ngrok's Cloud Endpoints /
  Traffic Policy API, a materially bigger change, out of scope here).
ARCHITECTURE PASS COMPLETE 2026-07-31 via multi-agent workflow (4 parallel designs -> synthesis ->
adversarial critique -> finalize). Full doc: docs/local-tunnel-multiplexer-architecture-2026-07-31.md

Headline finding beyond the original scope: session identity is NOT "one per process" on HTTP
transport (httpServer.ts builds a fresh Server per POST but tunnelManager is a bare module singleton)
-- naive single-Caddy-route-per-process would have let one HTTP caller's remote browser get routed
into a DIFFERENT caller's dev server. Fixed via a derived session key (hash of the caller's bearer
token) with each session key getting its own Caddy+tunnel; HTTP multi-replica deployments additionally
need session-affine LB routing as a documented go/no-go deployment precondition.

Also surfaced two pre-existing latent bugs (not new, but only exploitable once hostnames are shared
across ports/targets under this design) -- filed as new subtasks .6 and .7.

6 blocking review gaps found + fixed with real mechanisms + regression tests: queue-promotion race,
cold-start creation TOCTOU, HTTP multi-replica affinity, unspecified Host-header policy, unverified
trigger_crawl execution model, onPortChanged cleanup ordering. 6 more logged in doc SS6 as accepted
v1 tradeoffs (Caddy binary has no auto-installer -- biggest rollout risk, breaks zero-config promise
until documented or fast-followed; no cold-start progress signal; etc).

title: Health-probe failure tears down LIVE tunnels — 2 billed hours from an upstream fault
description:
Live today, before any other tunnel change. All handlers gate markTunnelDead on health.ngrokErrorCode (testPageChangesHandler.ts:318, probePageHandler.ts:186, triggerCrawlHandler.ts:171). Open bead kmzb documents that probeTunnelHealth cannot produce an ngrokErrorCode against this edge — a dead upstream returns an HTTP/2 GOAWAY, not ngrok's 502 interstitial — so the NGROK_ERROR arm at utils/localReachability.ts:215-227 is likely dead code.

Consequence: EVERY health-probe failure takes the else branch and calls plain stopTunnel.
- OWNED tunnel -> real disconnect + key revoke. The tunnel was probably fine; the probe usually fails because the USER'S DEV SERVER is unreachable. That is a 2-billed-hour teardown caused by an upstream fault.
- BORROWED tunnel -> leaves the shared registry entry intact, i.e. exactly the k34o gap the fix was meant to close.

ERR_NGROK_8012 makes it sharper: 8012 means the tunnel is ALIVE and refused the upstream — it is the tunnel that returned the error. Evicting on it orphans a live tunnel.

FIX: NETWORK_ERROR / TIMEOUT / BAD_GATEWAY / ERR_NGROK_8012 must leave the tunnel and registry entry ALONE and still return TunnelTrafficBlocked to the user; the user fixes their dev server and the next call reuses the tunnel free. Only codes proving the ENDPOINT is gone (ERR_NGROK_3200 + siblings, via an allowlist) may call markTunnelDead. Apply to all four handlers — runTestSuiteHandler.ts:105-119 never got the k34o treatment at all. Closing this should also close kmzb, since the fix removes the dependency on an ngrokErrorCode the probe cannot produce.

title: Tunnel registry path partitions on $TMPDIR — two MCPs keep two registries and always double-provision
description:
tunnelRegistry.ts:50 -> join(tmpdir(), 'debugg-ai-tunnels.json'). os.tmpdir() honours $TMPDIR, which varies by launch context: launchd per-user dir (/var/folders/.../T) vs a scrubbed env vs /tmp in the Docker image. Two MCP processes launched differently keep SEPARATE registries, never see each other's tunnels, and provision a duplicate per port — silently, forever. With a 1-hour minimum charge per tunnel that is a guaranteed, permanent double-bill, not an edge case.

Verified live 2026-07-27: os.tmpdir() = /var/folders/kg/sm6b47f91gg3s12lgtf35ht40000gn/T on this machine, so anything reading /tmp sees nothing. (That divergence also caused a false 'orphaned tunnel' diagnosis on bead lc62 — the trap is easy to fall into.)

FIX: pin the registry to a stable, launch-context-independent path — ~/.debugg-ai/tunnels.json — with a DEBUGG_AI_TUNNEL_REGISTRY override, and on first run migrate/merge any entry found at the legacy tmpdir() path.

Discovered-from lc62.

title: Registry freshness (30min) < tunnel idle-shutoff (55min) — 25min window that double-bills
description:
REGISTRY_FRESHNESS_TTL_MS = 30min gates borrowing; the tunnel itself idle-shuts-off at 55min. Between T+30 and T+55 the entry is judged unusable while the tunnel is still ALIVE and BILLING, so the next request provisions a second tunnel for the same port. With a 1-hour minimum charge per tunnel that is a systematic double-bill, not an edge case.

Either raise freshness to sit just under the idle-shutoff, or make the borrow decision probe the tunnel rather than infer liveness from a timestamp. Note isPidAlive() is a weak liveness proxy here specifically because sessions live for days (11 concurrent claude sessions observed, oldest 6d22h) — an alive owner PID says nothing about whether its tunnel survived.

title: check_app_in_browser: agent-loop node budgeted at 120s killed legitimate multi-step flows
description:
Client report: 3-step auth journeys (set password -> sign-in -> verify redirect) frequently hit 'Node timed out after 120s'. Splitting into separate MCP calls loses cross-step browser state, so it was not a workaround.

Cause: app_evaluation's eval_run_brain (the subworkflow.run wrapping the WHOLE browsing loop) declared no timeout and inherited WORKFLOW_NODE_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=120, while the brain subworkflow it runs is budgeted at 720s. The wrapper killed a subworkflow designed for 6x longer. The 120s default also retried once by default, re-running a loop that had already mutated server state.

Fix: timeout_budget.AGENT_LOOP_TIMEOUT_S=720 declared on eval_run_brain, policy max_retries=0, template version 6.4.0 -> 6.5.0.

title: [bug] check_app_in_browser re-borrows a DEAD tunnel on reuse (ERR_NGROK_3200 every call for 30min) — evict confirmed-dead entry from the shared registry
description:
The persistent ERR_NGROK_3200-on-reuse loop (the symptom that kept biting): every reuse/borrow gate
is a PROXY signal, never actual tunnel liveness.
  - isEntryUsable (borrow gate): owner-PID-alive + touched within REGISTRY_FRESHNESS_TTL_MS (30 min).
  - owned in-process reuse (getTunnelForPort, ~:199): NO check at all.
So when an ngrok tunnel dies out from under a still-alive process, the registry keeps calling it
"usable" and hands back a dead URL -> remote browser gets ERR_NGROK_3200. The merged z15n pre-flight
probe catches it, but stopTunnel on a BORROWED tunnel only drops the local ref and LEAVES the shared
cross-PID registry entry (tunnelManager.ts stopTunnel borrowed branch) — so every subsequent call,
in any session on that port, re-borrows the same corpse for up to 30 min. Owned tunnels self-healed
after one failure; borrowed did not.

FIX (committed 40b6753, branch fix/evict-dead-tunnel-on-reuse):
tunnelManager.markTunnelDead(port, tunnelId) — owned -> delegate to stopTunnel (already full
teardown); borrowed -> also evict the SHARED registry entry, guarded by tunnelId so a replacement
another session just provisioned is never removed. All 3 browser handlers (check_app_in_browser,
probe_page, trigger_crawl) call it INSTEAD of stopTunnel when the health probe returns an ngrok
tunnel-level marker (health.ngrokErrorCode / ERR_NGROK_*). A markerless failure (dev-server side)
still uses stopTunnel. Effect: "fails every call for 30 min" -> "fails once, next call re-provisions."

VERIFICATION: unit only. 855 tests pass. tunnelManager eviction tests RED without markTunnelDead;
handler wiring asserted (marker -> markTunnelDead not stopTunnel; markerless -> stopTunnel not
markTunnelDead) and RED if the handler branch is reverted. Mock factories across handler suites gained
markTunnelDead (additive; no assertions changed). NOT live-repro'd: manufacturing a real ERR_NGROK_3200
(kill an ngrok session while keeping a live registry entry) is exactly what the unit tests model;
proportionate to stop here, but a live recurrence repro would be the gold standard.

FOLLOW-UPS (not in this fix):
1. Transparent RECOVERY: on a dead reused tunnel, evict + re-provision + continue in the SAME call so
   even the first call succeeds (currently it still fails once). Bigger — retry path across 3 handlers.
2. Markerless dead: a dead tunnel that surfaces as NETWORK_ERROR (no ERR_NGROK_* marker) is NOT
   evicted (conservative, to avoid evicting a transiently-flaky-but-alive tunnel). Related to kmzb
   (the probe's marker behavior is edge-specific).
3. Root: the registry has no liveness signal at all (only PID + recency). Continuous liveness or a
   liveness field would prevent handing out a dead tunnel in the first place. Part of k34o audit.

Refs k34o (tunnel-layer audit), z15n (pre-flight probe), kmzb (probe marker behavior).
notes: MERGED + PUSHED to origin/main (merge af5a3a6, reconciled via 705df75, commit 40b6753). Unit-verified: 855 tests; tunnelManager eviction tests RED without markTunnelDead; handler wiring asserted both directions and RED if reverted; tsc/lint/build clean. Stops the RECURRENCE (borrowed dead tunnel no longer re-poisons the shared registry). Closing on unit verification — the full live ERR_NGROK_3200 recurrence was not manufactured (it's exactly what the unit tests model). Follow-ups remain OPEN as noted: (1) transparent recovery so even the first call self-heals; (2) markerless-dead eviction (kmzb); (3) registry has no liveness signal (k34o audit root).

title: cancel stops the workflow but leaves the browser session ACTIVE — eval_browser_teardown never runs, so the browser leaks
description:

/cancel/ — it has no way to tear down a browser session. If confirmed backend-owned, re-home to

cascade-cancel gap — this is likely the same root: terminal parent does not clean up children).

Do NOT assume it is fixable here. Verify ownership before writing code.

## TDD acceptance criteria

   re-fetch 511a3880 and/or query the browser session directly. If it is stale, this bead may be
   invalid; say so and close it. Do not build on an unverified field.
2. If real: reproduce — start a check_app_in_browser, cancel it, then poll the browser session and

3. Fix in whichever repo owns it, with a failing test first.
4. Live validation required before closing: cancel a real run, confirm the browser session is torn

Discovered-from debugg_ai_mcp-5er7.
notes:
=== INVESTIGATED 2026-07-15. Bead is VALID but MIS-SCOPED, and it is BACKEND-OWNED. Raising to P1. ===

## The headline was wrong; the bug underneath is worse

"The browser leaks" is WRONG. browserSession.status is a plain DB column on sentinal's BrowserSession,
written only by explicit lifecycle transitions (browser_sessions/session_monitor.py). NOTHING
reconciles it against browser-mgr — health_check_sessions_task only COUNTS rows, it never probes. So
status='ACTIVE' means "sentinal never wrote a terminal status", NOT "a browser is alive".
Confirmed empirically: exec 511a3880 still ACTIVE at ageSeconds 1104 then 1320 (22 min) — well past
browser-mgr's 600s TTL. The real browser is almost certainly long destroyed. The field is bookkeeping.

The REAL bug: the stale row permanently consumes a company concurrency slot.

## Verified chain (line-by-line, all confirmed independently)

1. app_evaluation.py:148 — eval_browser_teardown declares always_run: True.
2. The engine honors always_run ONLY on the FAILURE path: tasks.py:402, engine.py:435, engine.py:597
   — each guarded by `if outcome == "fail"`. The CANCEL path never runs it:
   cancel_workflow_execution_task (tasks.py:577) -> execution.cancel() (models.py:918) owns only the
   state transition; its own docstring concedes the gap. => always_run is honored on fail, SKIPPED on
   cancel. Empirically: exec 511a3880 = 4/5 nodes, eval_browser_teardown ABSENT.
3. Nothing reaps the ACTIVE row:
     - The ONLY scheduled browser-session reaper is "cleanup-orphaned-sessions"
       (config/settings/base.py:766, crontab */10). Its kwargs say "Terminate sessions pending >30
       minutes" and its docstring says "sessions stuck in PENDING/INITIALIZING" — it CANNOT see ACTIVE.
     - cleanup_orphaned_sessions_task (cleanup_tasks.py:215) — the good one: handles ACTIVE/PAUSED,
       calls end_session() — is exported in tasks/__init__.py but SCHEDULED NOWHERE.
     - browser_sessions/celery_config.py (which schedules cleanup_expired_sessions_task) has ZERO
       importers. Dead module; its schedule entries have never run. Verified by grep.
4. ACTIVE counts against the cap: session_monitor.py:435-443 counts
   status__in=[INITIALIZING, ACTIVE, PAUSED] per company vs MAX_CONCURRENT_BROWSER_SESSIONS
   (production.py:571, default 50).
5. HARD-ENFORCED: models/_managers.py:141-146 raises SessionLimitError
   ("Team has reached maximum concurrent sessions (N/50)").

=> Every cancelled run permanently burns 1 of 50 slots. ~50 cancels and the company can start NO
browser sessions at all. Cumulative, latent, self-inflicted DoS. Recordings/HARs are lost too:
_queue_recording_download is only reachable from end_session().

## Two INDEPENDENT bugs — fix both

A. Cancel must run the always_run pass (or finalize must, on every terminal transition).
B. The reaper wiring is broken, INDEPENDENT of cancel: schedule cleanup_orphaned_sessions_task
   (cleanup_tasks.py:215) and delete the dead browser_sessions/celery_config.py. ANY path that
   strands an ACTIVE row leaks a slot forever today, not just cancel.

## Relationship to the MCP side

This is what makes debugg_ai_mcp-5er7 (now reopened, P1) NET-NEGATIVE. Before 5er7 an abort left the
run going to its 720s budget — wasteful but bounded and self-healing, because teardown eventually ran.
After 5er7 an abort cancels, teardown is skipped, and a slot is burned permanently. Cancel is a brand
new path that 5er7 enabled, which is exactly why this has not bitten yet. The MCP relay only POSTs
/cancel/ — it has no lever here. NOT fixable in this repo.

## Sibling, not duplicate: sentinal-1e7wn

Different root, same fix site:
  - 1e7wn: child WorkflowExecutions keep EXECUTING and keep driving a browser. Fix = cascade-cancel.
  - ta96 : the parent's own always_run teardown is SKIPPED, so the row is never released.
Fixing either would not fix the other. Both want one "on terminal transition, do cleanup" hook.
BONUS — this confirms 1e7wn's previously-unproven inference: the even-2-minute sweeper is real:
workflows.check_execution_timeouts, crontab(minute="*/2"), config/settings/base.py:817.

## RECOMMENDATION

Re-home to sentinal as P1 (arguably P0 — it is a latent total-outage-per-company bug) and close this
bead as "wontfix — re-homed", NOT as invalid.

## Explicitly NOT verified

- Nobody confirmed browser-mgr actually destroyed session 33410. The ~10-15 min bound is INFERRED

  says ACTIVE at 22 min. A prod log check for destroy_session on that session would settle it.

title: REGRESSION (e20e20a): tunnel re-probe arm launders a genuine UI 'fail' into 'infrastructure' — probe answers 'healthy NOW?' but we claim 'was dead DURING the run'
description:
REGRESSION introduced by commit e20e20a (branch fix/cancel-abandoned-executions-tunnel-reclassify),
the z15n post-hoc reclassification. Found by live QA against prod, NOT by the unit tests.

## The bug

The re-probe arm has NO time-window awareness. It asks "is the tunnel healthy NOW?" and from that
concludes something about THE RUN WINDOW. Those are different questions. Result: a genuine UI
failure gets laundered into an infrastructure excuse — exactly what the fix was supposed to prevent
and what e20e20a's own commit message claims is impossible ("A healthy re-probe relays the verdict
untouched so a genuine UI failure is never laundered").

## Proof (live, prod, backend timestamps)

Execution 2aa14b0b-3a30-48e2-a646-65357cf775e2:
    completedAt : 2026-07-16T00:46:42.971669Z   durationMs=22298
    upstream killed at : 2026-07-16T00:46:45.752Z
    -> the execution COMPLETED 2.78s BEFORE the kill. The tunnel was ALIVE for the entire run.
    backend verdict : fail — "Evidence only shows a claimed text match for 'View Report'; it does
                      not verify the heading 'QA Throwaway App' is present."   (an honest
                      evidence-strictness verdict; nothing to do with tunnels)
    ERR_NGROK in evidence.actionTrace : NONE  (the marker arm did NOT fire)
    actionTrace proves the browser reached the REAL app: text_visible('View Report') — matched
    WE STILL EMITTED : error='TunnelOfflineDuringRun', failureCategory='infrastructure',
                       outcome='error'

Only the probe arm fired, and it fired solely because the probe ran AFTER the kill.

## This is not a rare race — the probe itself lies

Observed during the same QA session, on a demonstrably healthy server:
    [warn] Tunnel health probe failed for https://...ngrok.debugg.ai/: NETWORK_ERROR in 286ms
    $ curl http://127.0.0.1:39117/  ->  200
That was the PRE-FLIGHT probe racing DNS ~286ms after tunnel creation, ~1 in 5 runs. The identical
flake at POST-RUN probe time converts ANY genuine UI 'fail' into 'infrastructure'. So the false
positive is reachable without anyone killing anything.

## Why the unit tests missed it (important — don't repeat this)

__tests__/handlers/testPageChangesHandler.tunnelReclassify.test.ts MOCKS probeTunnelHealth. A
mocked probe is stipulated to be correct, so the suite structurally cannot express "the probe is
accurate about NOW but says nothing about the run window", nor "the probe flaked". The tests
validated the logic as written, not the assumption underneath it. Green tests were not evidence here.

## Secondary: 'unknown' is eligible for reclassification

2aa14b0b's backend outcome was literally `unknown`; services/verdictAdapter maps it to `fail`, so it
satisfied the `verdict.outcome === 'fail'` gate. `unknown` is even weaker grounds for asserting an
infrastructure fault than `fail` is.

## Suggested fix

REQUIRE the ERR_NGROK_* marker; demote the re-probe to corroboration/detail only, never sufficient
on its own. Rationale from the QA data:
  - True positive (real mid-run death): BOTH arms fired (re-probe=NETWORK_ERROR, marker=ERR_NGROK_3200).
    Marker-only still catches it. Confirmed: a real mid-run death DOES surface the marker in
    evidence.actionTrace, independently of the verdict reason.
  - False positive (2aa14b0b): NO marker. Marker-only relays it verbatim. Bug gone.
The marker is positive evidence the remote browser actually hit OUR error page DURING the run —
which is the claim we're making. The probe is evidence about now. Per epic 56kd, only the former
justifies overriding the backend.

Alternative if the probe arm must be kept: gate it on evidence the tunnel was unreachable BEFORE
completedAt. Harder, and no data source for it today.

## TDD acceptance criteria

1. FAILING TEST FIRST reproducing 2aa14b0b's exact shape: healthy run, genuine backend 'fail'
   (evidence-strictness reason), NO ERR_NGROK marker anywhere, probe returns unhealthy/NETWORK_ERROR.
   Assert the verdict is relayed VERBATIM — no reclassification, no `error` key, no `backendVerdict`.
   This test MUST fail against current HEAD (e20e20a) before the fix.
2. Existing true-positive test (marker present) must still pass — no coverage regression.
3. Test: outcome 'unknown' + no marker + unhealthy probe -> relayed verbatim.
4. Test: marker present + probe healthy -> still reclassifies (marker is the authority).
5. Full suite green: npm test, npx tsc --noEmit, npm run lint, npm run build.
6. Live re-validation against prod required before closing (see debugg_ai_mcp-z15n): reproduce a real
   mid-run tunnel death and confirm it STILL reclassifies, and reproduce a healthy-run genuine fail
   and confirm it does NOT. Unit tests alone are explicitly NOT sufficient for this bead — mocked
   probes are what caused it.

Blocks debugg_ai_mcp-z15n. Relates to epic debugg_ai_mcp-56kd ("relay honestly, invent nothing") —
asserting an infrastructure fault we did not observe during the run is the relay inventing a cause.
close_reason: FIXED in commit 8f42094 and live-validated both directions. The ERR_NGROK_* marker is now REQUIRED to reclassify; the post-run re-probe is demoted to corroboration (recorded in detail, cannot trigger reclassification on its own). LIVE PROOF regression gone: bf628842-6091-4086-bd58-23b47e46ec3e — run completed 0.22s BEFORE the upstream kill (tunnel alive throughout), post-run probe returned the exact NETWORK_ERROR that previously triggered laundering, backend outcome=fail with NO marker in actionTrace; we relayed outcome=fail verbatim, no error key, no backendVerdict. LIVE PROOF no coverage lost: fb3f832f-0b5d-4ce2-b613-9c0352609492 — real mid-run tunnel death, marker ERR_NGROK_8012 present in evidence.actionTrace, still reclassified to TunnelOfflineDuringRun/infrastructure with backendVerdict preserved. Independently verified: 830 tests pass; reverting the source makes 4 of the new tests fail; ZERO assertion deletions in the pre-existing test (only its fixture was corrected — it had encoded the bug and was physically incoherent). New tests encode a probe that is WRONG rather than merely unhealthy, including a property test that flaky and healthy probes yield an identical payload — the gap that let the original mocked-probe suite miss this. NOTE: only ERR_NGROK_3200 and _8012 are live-confirmed codes; the regex matches any ERR_NGROK_\d+.

title: cancelExecution() is dead code — client abort stops our poll but leaves the backend execution running (burns a browser session + quota with nobody reading the result)
description:
services/workflows.ts declares (:159) and implements (:245) cancelExecution(), which POSTs api/v1/workflows/executions/<uuid>/cancel/. It has ZERO callers anywhere in the repo:

    grep -rn 'cancelExecution' --include='*.ts' . | grep -v node_modules | grep -v ./dist
    -> only the interface decl + the impl. No call sites.

Meanwhile testPageChangesHandler.ts:129-138 wires context.signal to an AbortController so a
client cancel/transport drop aborts pollExecution. The comment at :121-128 explains the intent:
a dropped client used to keep polling ~10 min and hold one of just MAX_CONCURRENT=2 slots, so
aborting frees the slot immediately.

That fixed the SLOT leak but not the WORK leak. On abort we stop polling and free the slot, but
the backend execution is never cancelled — it keeps running to completion (contextData
timeoutSeconds=720, so up to ~12 min), driving a real browser session, burning runner time and
quota, with nobody reading the result.

## Repro / evidence

Not reproduced by cancelling a live call (worth doing before fixing). Evidence is code-level:
zero call sites for a function that exists precisely for this, plus the abort path only
touching the poll.

Adjacent (backend-owned, tracked in sentinal-1e7wn, NOT this bug): when a parent app-eval
execution reaches terminal state, its brain subworkflows are not cascade-cancelled and keep
driving browsers ~8-11 min after the parent returned (parent aa9bef1b returned 01:19:18;
brains bd9c04cb/52c2f382 ran to 01:28:00/01:30:00). Same family of leak, different owner —
that one we cannot fix from the relay because the parent had already finished on its own.

## Suggested fix

On abort (and on any path where we abandon an execution we queued), call
client.workflows.cancelExecution(executionUuid) best-effort before returning. Guard it:
fire-and-forget with a short timeout and swallow errors, since by definition the client is
already gone and we must not throw from the abort path or delay slot release.

Verify with: start a check_app_in_browser, cancel the MCP request, then poll
executions action:get on the returned executionId and assert it reaches status 'cancelled'
rather than continuing to 'completed'.
notes:
=== REOPENED 2026-07-15 — this fix is NET-NEGATIVE as shipped. DO NOT RELEASE e20e20a's cancel path yet. ===

I closed this as 'FIXED + LIVE-VALIDATED'. That was wrong. The cancel POST does work (verified:
execution 511a3880 reached status='cancelled' 292ms after abort). But that validated the narrow
claim "does cancel work?" and missed the systemic consequence: CANCELLING SKIPS THE BROWSER
TEARDOWN, and the resulting BrowserSession row leaks a company concurrency slot PERMANENTLY.

Verified chain (read line-by-line from sentinal source):

1. app_evaluation.py:148 declares eval_browser_teardown with always_run: True.

2. The engine honors always_run ONLY on the failure path — tasks.py:402, engine.py:435,
   engine.py:597, each guarded by: if outcome == "fail". cancel_workflow_execution_task
   (tasks.py:577) -> execution.cancel() (models.py:918) performs the STATE TRANSITION ONLY and
   never runs the always_run pass. So teardown is skipped on cancel.
   Confirmed empirically: exec 511a3880 shows 4/5 nodes, eval_browser_teardown ABSENT.

3. The row is then never reaped. The ONLY scheduled browser-session reaper is
   "cleanup-orphaned-sessions" (config/settings/base.py:766, every 10 min) and it handles
   PENDING/INITIALIZING only — its own kwargs say "Terminate sessions pending >30 minutes".
   The ACTIVE-aware reaper cleanup_orphaned_sessions_task (cleanup_tasks.py:215) is exported but
   scheduled NOWHERE. browser_sessions/celery_config.py (which would schedule
   cleanup_expired_sessions_task) has ZERO importers — dead module, verified by grep.

4. ACTIVE counts against the cap: session_monitor.py:435-443 counts
   status__in=[INITIALIZING, ACTIVE, PAUSED] per company against
   MAX_CONCURRENT_BROWSER_SESSIONS (production.py:571, default 50).

5. It is HARD-ENFORCED: models/_managers.py:141-146 raises SessionLimitError when can_start_new
   is false ("Team has reached maximum concurrent sessions (N/50)").

NET EFFECT OF THIS "FIX":
  BEFORE — an abort left the execution running to its 720s budget. Wasteful, but teardown
           eventually ran, the session ended, and the slot was returned. BOUNDED + SELF-HEALING.
  AFTER  — an abort cancels, teardown is skipped, the row sits ACTIVE forever and burns 1 of 50
           slots. UNBOUNDED + CUMULATIVE. ~50 aborts => that company can start NO browser sessions
           at all. A self-inflicted DoS. Cancel is a brand-new path that only this fix enabled,
           which is exactly why nobody has hit it yet.

Recordings/HARs are also permanently lost on cancelled runs (null recordingUrl/harUrl): the
download is only queued from end_session(), which teardown would have called.

Note the real browser itself IS bounded — browser-mgr reaps it on its own ~600s TTL. The leak is
the sentinal DB row, and the DB row is what the quota counts. So "the browser self-heals" is true
and irrelevant.

BLOCKED ON the sentinal-side fix (run the always_run pass on cancel, and/or schedule an
ACTIVE-aware reaper). See debugg_ai_mcp-ta96, being re-homed to sentinal.

OPTIONS until then:
  (a) hold e20e20a's cancel path out of any release
  (b) gate it behind an env flag, default OFF
  (c) ship anyway and accept burning a slot per abort
Recommendation: (a) or (b). The disease this cures is bounded and self-healing; the cure is not.
MERGED to main INERT (2026-07-17, merge 196c42d, gate commit 3d47ce7). The cancel-on-abort code and its mechanism tests are on main, but gated behind DEBUGGAI_CANCEL_ABANDONED_EXECUTIONS (read at call time, DEFAULT OFF). Shipped behaviour = pre-fix: the poll aborts and frees our slot, the backend runs to its 720s budget, teardown runs, the slot returns — bounded and self-healing. A new test pins this default (abort frees the slot, cancelExecution NOT called). DO NOT flip the flag to 'true' until sentinal-wmzdf lands (backend must run the always_run teardown on cancel); until then, enabling it trades a bounded waste for a permanent per-company slot leak. This bead stays OPEN as the flip-the-flag tracker, blocked on sentinal-wmzdf. The other four (z15n, 4bui, pqgj, k6yq) are merged ACTIVE.

title: [bug][BACKEND-NOT-MCP] verify-gate reads Next.js's route-announcer (role=alert) as a blocking error — page TITLE fails every passing run
description:
check_app_in_browser returns outcome='fail' for a page that rendered and behaved correctly. The failure reason quotes the app's own HTML <title> as if it were an error banner:

    reason: "verify-gate: claimed success but the page shows a blocking error — DebuggAI - LLM Application Debugger"

'DebuggAI - LLM Application Debugger' is the <title> of every authenticated page in react-web-app. Nothing on the page is an error. The browser agent itself reported success at the prior step; the verify-gate then overrode it and flipped the run to fail.

Strong suspicion: the gate scans page text/title for error-ish keywords and 'Debugger' (or 'Debug') trips the heuristic. This makes check_app_in_browser structurally unable to return 'pass' for OUR OWN product, whose name contains the trigger word — i.e. every DebuggAI dashboard verification is a guaranteed false negative.

## Context
Hit twice while visually verifying a react-web-app canvas UI change (crawl knowledge-graph map) on 2026-07-14.

Reproductions (both returned outcome=fail with a CORRECT, fully-rendered page in the screenshot):
  - executionId 8d308bd7-9299-475f-8d75-2dc43b7c4e93 (durationMs 85240, stepsTaken 3)
  - executionId 0f09848c-9ac8-4c3d-a77a-cfb2463da72f (durationMs 63135, stepsTaken 2)

Target: http://localhost:3011/projects/83fa71e2-ff6d-4cc3-9c19-272b024f08fa/graphs (localhost tunnel)
resolvedEnvironmentId: f9ee0391-b3da-4fc8-be38-4ba523d69483
Browser sessions: 994757fa-6dd1-454e-92a2-627041be60d7 / acb67e6a-fcbc-488d-b42d-226f7beb0fce
Server: debugg-ai-published (npx @latest).

In the 0f09848c trace, step 1 = click, success:true, intent 'the map is visible and ready for evaluation'; step 2 = done, success:false with the title-as-error reason. The screenshot from that same run shows the map fully rendered (84 pages / 1306 edges) with the settings panel open.

IMPACT: a human has to eyeball the screenshot to discover the run actually passed, which defeats the point of an automated gate and trains users to ignore 'fail'.
design:
Likely fix is server-side (the verify-gate / judge that post-processes the agent's done step), not in the MCP relay itself — but filing here since this is the surface users hit. Suggestions:
  1. Don't treat <title> (or any static chrome) as page error text — a blocking error should be a rendered error state (error boundary, 4xx/5xx body, empty root), not a substring match.
  2. If keyword matching is kept, match on error SEMANTICS in visible body content, and never on the document title. At minimum stop matching bare 'Debugger'/'Debug'.
  3. When the gate overrides the agent's own success verdict, the reason should quote WHERE it saw the error (selector + text), so the false positive is debuggable from the trace alone.
Relates to epic debugg_ai_mcp-56kd ('relay honestly, invent nothing') — reporting a title as a blocking error is the gate inventing a failure.
notes: ## CORRECTION 2026-07-15 — root cause PROVEN; my original theory was WRONG, and this is NOT an MCP bug I originally guessed 'the gate keyword-matches the and trips on the word Debugger'. That is WRONG. Proven mechanism below. ### This lives in sentinal, not this repo - Emitter: sentinal backend/backend/workflows/node_executors/_brain_act_verify.py:50 return f"claimed success but the page shows a blocking error — {blocking_errors[0]}" - The gate does NO keyword matching. It blindly trusts a blocking_errors list passed in. - Producer: sentinal backend/backend/surfers/control/controller.py:185 blocking_errors() - Selector: controller.py:80 _ERROR_SELECTOR — first entry is [role="alert"] - This MCP repo contains ZERO occurrences of 'claimed success'. It only relays the backend's outcome verbatim (services/workflows.ts:236, handlers/triggerCrawlHandler.ts:296). Nothing here can produce or suppress this verdict. ### The actual bug Next.js App Router ships <next-route-announcer>, an a11y live region that announces route changes to screen readers by setting its text to document.title. It renders as: <next-route-announcer>#shadow-root<div role="alert">{page title}</div> _ERROR_SELECTOR's [role="alert"] scoops it up, so blocking_errors() returns the PAGE TITLE as a blocking error, and the verify-gate downgrades a genuine success to fail. ### Reproduced live (Playwright, sentinal's exact _ERROR_SELECTOR, 2026-07-15) A) right after a client-side route change (login redirect): title : "Dashboard | DebuggAI - LLM Application Debugger" matches : [{where:"shadow:next-route-announcer", role:"alert", text:"Dashboard | DebuggAI - LLM Application Debugger"}] <-- THE BUG B) after a hard navigation (goto) -> announcer text "" (0 real error elements) C) 1.2s after a later client-side nav -> announcer text "" D) 4s later -> announcer text "" Light-DOM matches for _ERROR_SELECTOR on the loaded app: 0. The ONLY match is the announcer. ### Why this matters far more than I first wrote 1. It is a RACE, not a constant: the announcer holds the title only briefly after a client-side nav. That is exactly why only some runs fail (and why it looks like flake). 2. It is NOT DebuggAI-specific. EVERY Next.js App Router app has next-route-announcer. Any customer Next.js app verified by check_app_in_browser can have its page title reported as a blocking error if the surfer samples blocking_errors() in that window. The 'our product name contains Debugger' framing was a red herring — the title's CONTENT is irrelevant; any non-empty title trips it. ### Fix (in sentinal) 1. Exclude the announcer: next-route-announcer, [aria-live] live regions, and any role=alert inside them are ANNOUNCEMENTS, not blocking errors. 2. Better: don't treat bare [role="alert"] as blocking on its own — it is the generic a11y role for toasts/announcements. Require error semantics (aria-invalid, an error class, or association with a form control). 3. Ignore text equal to document.title — an 'error' identical to the page title is never a real validation error. 4. blocking_errors() should record WHICH element/selector produced the hit so the trace is debuggable without a live repro. ACTION: re-file against sentinal (surfers/control + workflows verify-gate) and close this as moved. Keeping it open here only tracks the hand-off.
close_reason: MIS-FILED — not this repo's bug. Re-homed to sentinal-qs8cr (epic: blocking_errors() reports NON-errors as blocking errors). The relay has zero verdict logic: it relays outcome verbatim via services/verdictAdapter; grep for 'claimed success' here = 0 hits. Root cause CONFIRMED live: Next.js App Router's <next-route-announcer> renders <div role=alert> whose text is document.title, inside an OPEN shadow root that Playwright's CSS engine pierces; sentinal's _ERROR_SELECTOR leads with [role=alert], so blocking_errors()[0] returns the page TITLE and _brain_act_verify.py:50 downgrades a real success. Also a REGRESSION from sentinal f50e52b7 (2026-07-13T20:58:09Z, 'wire verify-gate into the app-eval provider path'): last pass 19d16ec5 predates it by 72min; every run after fails. This bead's original theory (keyword-matching 'Debugger' in the title) was wrong — the title is set globally for every route and was present on the passing run too.

title: Review: audit tunnel layer for request-scoped-state-on-shared-record siblings, port-only tunnel identity, and the silent path substitution that made probe_page mis-report for a day
description:
Companion audit to debugg_ai_mcp-zmc9 (P0 fix). zmc9 fixes ONE field at three call sites.
This bead asks the two questions zmc9 deliberately does not: (a) is the same class of
mistake elsewhere in the tunnel layer, and (b) why did the MCP actively hide the truth for
~a day and produce four wrong root causes? A tool whose job is to report what the browser
saw mis-reported what the browser saw, confidently. That is a correctness bug in the
product's core promise, independent of the tunnel fix.

Scope this as a READ + PROPOSE pass. Land findings as child beads; do not bundle unrelated
fixes into zmc9.

## A. The bug class: request-scoped state cached on tunnel-scoped records

zmc9's root cause is `publicUrl` (origin + PATH — request-scoped) persisted onto a
`TunnelInfo` / registry entry keyed only by PORT (tunnel-scoped). Audit for siblings:

1. `TunnelInfo.originalUrl` (`services/ngrok/tunnelManager.ts:60`-ish decl; written at
   `:362` on BORROW as `originalUrl: url`). This is also request-scoped state living on a
   shared record. On borrow it is overwritten with the borrower's URL while the record is
   shared. Ask: who reads `originalUrl` after borrow, and can a second borrower observe the
   first borrower's value? Same shape as zmc9.
2. Enumerate every field on `TunnelInfo` and the registry entry and classify each as
   tunnel-scoped (id, origin, port, ownerPid, timers) vs request-scoped (path, search,
   hash, originalUrl). Anything in the second class must not be cached or returned.
3. `grep -rn "publicUrl" --include=*.ts .` (excluding dist/node_modules) and confirm zmc9
   caught ALL consumers, not just the three known sites. A fourth site reintroduces the bug.
4. Recommend the structural fix over the pointwise one: if the registry stores only
   `tunnelUrl` + `tunnelId` + `port` + liveness, the defect becomes unrepresentable.

## B. Tunnel identity: is PORT a sufficient key?

`findExistingTunnel` / `processUrl` key on `extractLocalhostPort()` alone.

5. Do `localhost:3011`, `127.0.0.1:3011`, `[::1]:3011`, and `0.0.0.0:3011` collapse to the
   same key? They are different origins. If they collapse, a tunnel created for one is
   handed to a caller asking for another — a same-class identity bug with a different field
   (host instead of path).
6. Do scheme differences (`http` vs `https` on the same port) collapse?
7. Is `ownerPid` + freshness TTL (`isEntryUsable`, bead 3th) sufficient given a shared
   `$TMPDIR` file? Consider concurrent writes: `reg.read()` → mutate → `reg.write(registry)`
   at `:355-373` is read-modify-write with no visible locking. With N sessions (this box
   routinely runs 6+), can two borrowers interleave and clobber an entry? Check
   `tunnelRegistry.ts` for atomic write / lockfile.

## C. Diagnosability — the part that actually cost the day

8. `utils/tunnelContext.ts:110+` `sanitizeResponse()` rewrites tunnel URLs back to the
   original localhost origin. Consequence observed: the WRONG path was reported under the
   RIGHT origin (`http://localhost:3011/projects/.../graphs`), which reads exactly like the
   app performed its own redirect. Every investigator concluded "the app is redirecting" and
   went hunting app-side (routing, returnTo, auth, browser state, .env) — four times.
   Proposal: sanitize the ORIGIN for cosmetics, but never let sanitization make a
   substituted path look like a caller-requested one.
9. Requested-vs-actual mismatch must be LOUD, not silent. In the repro, `finalUrl` was
   sanitized while the `error` string leaked the truth
   (`navigating to "http://localhost:3011/projects/83fa71e2-.../graphs"`) — the two fields
   disagreed and only the error was honest. Had the timeout not fired, there would have been
   NO signal at all: a successful probe of the wrong page reports as a successful probe.
   Propose: when the resolved target's path != the requested path, either refuse or surface
   an explicit warning + both URLs in the result. Silent substitution is never acceptable in
   a verification tool.
10. Add a `requestedUrl` alongside `finalUrl` in probe_page / check_app_in_browser results
    so callers can always see the delta themselves.
11. Telemetry already tags `TUNNEL_PROVISIONED { how: 'reused' | 'borrowed' }`
    (`tunnelManager.ts:332/375`). Cheap win: also tag whether the reused target's path
    differed from the request. That would have surfaced this in aggregate on day one, and
    can measure blast radius in the wild retroactively.

## D. Blast radius (answer before closing)

12. Every tool that tunnels localhost is affected, not just probe_page: `triggerCrawlHandler`

title: Remote browser leaks session state across 'fresh' check_app_in_browser/probe_page runs — stale navigation/returnTo poisons verification
description:
The remote browser driving check_app_in_browser / probe_page (published MCP 3.7.0) carries persisted state (localStorage / cookies / IndexedDB / history / service-worker) ACROSS separate tool invocations against the same app, even though each call reports a DISTINCT browserSession UUID. Result: a route from a PRIOR run gets injected into later 'fresh' runs, so verification silently reports app behavior that ISN'T real.

PROVEN via local-vs-remote A/B on the SAME app (react-web-app on http://localhost:3011, unauthenticated, no committed redirect to the leaked path):

  Route                    | LOCAL fresh browser (Playwright)          | MCP REMOTE browser
  -------------------------|-------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------
  /                        | -> /login              (CLEAN, correct)   | -> /login?returnTo=%2Ftest-knowledge-graph  (WRONG)
  /login                   | -> /login                                 | -> /login?returnTo=%2Ftest-knowledge-graph  (WRONG)
  /test-knowledge-graph    | -> /login?returnTo=%2Ftest-knowledge-graph| same

Same code, same URLs, only the browser env differs. Locally, GET / redirects to a clean /login (exactly what the source dictates: the auth guard on '/' emits /login with NO returnTo). The '/test-knowledge-graph' string exists NOWHERE in the app source (grep across all file types = one code comment), yet the remote browser injects it as a returnTo on '/' and even on '/login'. It is a leftover from EARLIER KG-verification runs against this same app.

Isolation is fake: three separate probe_page calls returned distinct browserSession UUIDs (a48fdb62..., 8604f903..., 055d360c...) yet ALL injected the identical stale /test-knowledge-graph — so a new session UUID does NOT mean a clean profile/storage.

Ruled out (so this is squarely the remote-browser env, not the app or MCP transport): tool/URL-replay artifact, client returnTo persistence (none in source), stale local dev server (full kill + rm -rf .next + restart reproduced it), stale .next cache, mock mode (off). MCP transport itself is healthy — it faithfully reports whatever its browser did.

IMPACT (why P1): silent wrong verification. An agent using check_app_in_browser to confirm UI/redirect/auth behavior gets a finalUrl that reflects stale cross-run state, not the app. Cost a multi-hour false investigation ('stale returnTo' goose chase) and undermines trust in the tool for anything auth/redirect/navigation-related.

FIX DIRECTION: guarantee a truly ephemeral browser context per execution — no shared localStorage/cookies/IndexedDB/service-worker/history/profile-dir across runs (or key the profile per-execution and tear it down). Investigate whether the remote browser reuses a profile dir keyed by app/project/tunnel-origin.

RELATED (separate, note not fix here): the remote browser cannot reach a local-only backend — the tunnel exposes the app port (:3011) but the client bundle calls NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8012, which on the remote browser is ITS OWN localhost. So authed flows against a purely-local stack can't be verified via the published tunnel (also why it 'couldn't get past login'). Worth its own bead if not already tracked.
close_reason:
NOT A BUG — misdiagnosed. Root cause was a react-web-app .env.local override (NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8012) defeating the same-origin /api/proxy default, so the client bundle told the REMOTE browser to call its own localhost:8012 (unreachable) and the app fell into a bogus /test-knowledge-graph route state. There is NO browser session-state leak: browser-mgr is container-per-session single-use (ephemeral per-session --user-data-dir, terminated at session end), so sessions never share a browser.

DECISIVE A/B (same probe_page url=http://localhost:3011/, only .env changed):
  BEFORE: finalUrl /login?returnTo=%2Ftest-knowledge-graph; network shows /test-knowledge-graph 200 and NO request for '/'; loads app_(dashboard)_test-knowledge-graph_page_tsx.
  AFTER : finalUrl /login; network shows '/' 200 and NO /test-knowledge-graph; loads app_(dashboard)_page_tsx.
The MCP was faithful the whole time — it accurately reported a real (environment-induced) app state. Real fix tracked as react-web-app-4aca. sentinal-ew37m closed (false premise). sentinal-6qz1t fixed a non-problem (harmless defensive hardening only).

comments.author: Quinn
comments.text: ROOT CAUSE FOUND + work epic opened in sentinal: sentinal-6qz1t (browser_sessions per-session context isolation). The pooled CDP browser reuses contexts[0] (playwright_adapter.py:65) and teardown only clear_cookies() (browser.py:45), so localStorage/history leak across sessions. Fix + TDD tracked there; keep this open until the sentinal fix lands and sequential probes verify clean.

comments.author: Quinn
comments.text: CORRECTION (evidence from browser-mgr): sessions do NOT share browsers — browser-mgr is container-per-session, single-use (per-session ephemeral --user-data-dir, container terminated at session end, no shared profile volume; lifecycle_tasks.py:463/483, warm_pool LPOP claim). So the /test-knowledge-graph appearing across THREE distinct-UUID probe sessions CANNOT be cross-session browser-state leak. That means the 'browser session state leak' root cause here is likely misdiagnosed, and sentinal-6qz1t (storage-clear on fresh CDP connect) — while valid defensive hardening — probably does NOT fix this symptom. Real cause is upstream SEEDING of /test-knowledge-graph per run (candidate: project/app-eval stored start-url or returnTo, or the probe/tunnel path), not the browser. Do NOT close on 6qz1t deploy alone. Next: run the MCP probe A/B after 6qz1t hits staging; if /test-knowledge-graph persists (expected), re-investigate the seeder — sentinal app-eval/probe target resolution + any per-project stored returnTo — NOT the browser layer. sentinal-ew37m closed (browser-mgr recycle = false premise, already single-use).

title: Fix: finally block cleanup order and missing awaits
description:
testPageChangesHandler.ts finally block has two problems:

Problem 1 — wrong order:
  revokeNgrokKey(ngrokKeyId).catch(...)   ← fires first
  releaseTunnel(ctx).catch(...)           ← fires second

revokeNgrokKey revokes the short-lived ngrok API key. If this runs before releaseTunnel, the ngrok disconnect() call inside releaseTunnel operates on an already-invalidated session → disconnect fails → the TunnelInfo entry stays in activeTunnels map → next call finds stale entry.

Problem 2 — both fire-and-forget:
  Neither is awaited. If the user immediately calls the tool again, the second call can start while cleanup from the first is still pending. The second ngrok.authtoken() call (if not fixed by x5e) can disrupt the first call's disconnect.

Fix:
  await releaseTunnel(ctx)         ← disconnect first
  revokeNgrokKey(ngrokKeyId)...    ← revoke after tunnel is cleanly closed

The key revocation is backend housekeeping and can remain fire-and-forget. The tunnel disconnect must complete first.
close_reason: Implemented.

title: Fix: remove global ngrok.authtoken() call
description:
tunnelManager.ts calls ngrok.authtoken({ authtoken }) as a global setter before every connect(). This is dangerous:

1. The ngrok JS SDK stores this in a global config file (~/.ngrok2/ngrok.yml or similar)
2. Concurrent or rapid-sequential calls with different keys overwrite each other's global state
3. The authtoken is ALREADY passed directly in connect() options — the global call is redundant

Fix: remove the ngrok.authtoken() call entirely from both createSharedTunnel() (line ~316) and createTunnel() (line ~447). The authtoken in the connect options is sufficient.

Before:
  await ngrok.authtoken({ authtoken: authToken });
  const tunnelUrl = await ngrok.connect({ proto: 'http', addr, hostname, authtoken: authToken });

After:
  const tunnelUrl = await ngrok.connect({ proto: 'http', addr, hostname, authtoken: authToken });

Test: run two rapid sequential processUrl() calls and verify both succeed without authtoken interference.
close_reason: Implemented.

title: Investigate: tunnel flaking on subsequent sessions
description:
Users report: first check_app_in_browser call on a localhost URL succeeds, subsequent calls fail. Need to confirm which failure mode is triggering in production logs.

Hypotheses to verify (in order of likelihood):

1. ngrok.authtoken() global state race
   - Every processUrl() call does ngrok.authtoken({ authtoken: newKey }) BEFORE connect()
   - This sets global config on the ngrok daemon process
   - Call 1 is in its finally block (fire-and-forget releaseTunnel), Call 2 starts and calls authtoken(key2)
   - key2 overwrites the global ngrok session, potentially killing Call 1's still-running disconnect
   - Code: tunnelManager.ts lines 316 and 447

2. Key revoked before tunnel disconnected
   - finally block order: revokeNgrokKey(ngrokKeyId) THEN releaseTunnel(ctx)
   - Both fire-and-forget (.catch(), no await)
   - Key revocation invalidates the ngrok session → disconnect() on that session fails → stale entry left in activeTunnels
   - Next call for same port: findTunnelByPort() returns stale entry with dead URL

3. activeTunnels stale entry after failed cleanup
   - If releaseTunnel fails (because key was already revoked), activeTunnels still has the entry
   - Next call: findTunnelByPort(3000) returns the stale TunnelInfo → handler tries to use dead tunnel URL → backend browser can't navigate

Investigation steps:
- Add detailed logging around authtoken/connect/disconnect calls
- Check what error the backend returns on second call (404? connection refused? ngrok 4xx?)
- Check if activeTunnels has a stale entry on the second call
- Check if releaseTunnel is throwing on the first call (logging .catch output)
